query: Which material can be used for superconducting properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high-entropy alloy based on Nb, Mo, Ta, and W (e.g., NbMoTaW) will exhibit superconducting behavior at sufficiently low temperatures because the presence of Nb and Ta can enable electron pairing via conventional electron‐phonon coupling, even within the disordered but crystalline BCC matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbMoTaW fabricated as a single-phase BCC solid solution via methods such as selective laser melting or laser powder bed fusion.
generation.intervention: Cool the material down to cryogenic temperatures (e.g., below 10 K) while subjecting it to electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements.
generation.conditions: Measurements should be performed in a zero- or low-magnetic-field environment and under well-controlled cryogenic conditions to detect any superconducting transition.
generation.structural_mediator: The homogeneous BCC lattice with inherent lattice distortion and any short-range ordering that minimizes atomic displacements may facilitate an electron-phonon coupling environment, similar to that found in conventional Nb- and Ta-based superconductors.
generation.mechanism: Superconductivity is anticipated to emerge via conventional electron–phonon coupling mediated pairing. The high concentration of Nb (and to a lesser extent Ta) in the alloy, despite the disordered high-entropy configuration, can support Cooper pair formation once thermal agitation is sufficiently suppressed.
generation.predicted_outcome: Below a critical temperature (likely in the few Kelvin range), the material will exhibit a sharp drop to zero electrical resistance along with the onset of a diamagnetic response (Meissner effect).
generation.baseline: At temperatures above the superconducting transition, the alloy behaves as a normal metallic conductor with finite resistivity.
generation.boundary: The superconducting properties may be sensitive to processing-induced defects, residual stresses, and variations in short-range order. Excessive disorder or impurity phases might suppress or broaden the transition.
generation.uncertainty: Direct evidence for superconductivity in NbMoTaW HEAs is not available in the provided records; the hypothesis extrapolates from the known superconducting properties of elemental Nb and Ta. The influence of the high-entropy, disordered state on electron scattering and pairing remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of NbMoTaW using established additive manufacturing techniques to obtain a homogeneous BCC phase. Cool the samples in a dilution refrigerator and perform four-probe electrical resistivity measurements while simultaneously measuring magnetic susceptibility. The experiment should span a temperature range from above 10 K down to at least 1 K.
measurements: Electrical resistivity as a function of temperature to detect a transition to zero resistance.
Magnetic susceptibility (using AC susceptibility or SQUID magnetometry) to observe the onset of the Meissner effect.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no abrupt drop in resistivity to zero and no measurable diamagnetic response are observed down to the lowest temperature (≈1 K), then the hypothesis that the NbMoTaW high-entropy alloy exhibits superconductivity is falsified.

Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
